title: An Horatian Ode: occasion, date, publication
short: Written in summer 1650, after Cromwell returned from Ireland (late May) and before he invaded Scotland (22 July); cancelled from most copies of the 1681 Poems.
body: Cromwell returned to London from his Irish campaign at the end of May 1650 and in July led the army into Scotland, where the Scots had proclaimed Charles II. The poem looks back to the regicide of January 1649 and forward to the Scottish war, so it is dated June-July 1650. It was printed in Marvell's Miscellaneous Poems (1681) but cancelled in all but one or two surviving copies, presumably because praise of Cromwell was dangerous after the Restoration; it reached most readers only in Thompson's edition (1776). The archive's title keeps the old spellings 'Horation' and 'Cromwel'.

title: The Horatian stanza
short: Four-line stanzas of two tetrameter and two trimeter lines in couplets, an English imitation of the Horatian ode stanza.
body: Each stanza pairs a couplet of four-stress lines with a shorter couplet of three-stress lines, producing a clipped, falling cadence that is an English stanza, not a Latin metre, but it aims at the compression of Horace's lyric stanzas. Horace's political odes, praising Augustus after the Roman civil wars (Odes 1.2, 1.37, 3.1-6, 4.4-5), supply the model of a poem that celebrates a strongman while remembering the defeated: Odes 1.37 honours Cleopatra's noble death as Marvell honours Charles's. The opening stanzas urge the ambitious young man to leave poetry for action.

title: The forward Youth
short: An ambitious young man eager to make his mark; possibly a glance at Marvell himself, poised between poetry and public life.
body: 'Forward' means eager, ambitious, even presumptuous. 'Appear' means to make a public showing. Such a youth must leave 'the Shadows' (the shade of retirement, also the poet's pastoral shade) and his 'Numbers languishing' (love verses). The armour 'of the Hall' was the family armour hung up on the walls of a country house; 'Corslet' is body armour. Many critics see Marvell, then about twenty-nine and without employment, addressing his own situation; others think of young royalists or the generation called to arms.

title: his active Star
short: Cromwell, unable to rest in peace, drove on his destiny; his 'Star' is the astrological fortune that both governs and is urged by him.
body: The verb 'urged' makes Cromwell the master of his destiny rather than its servant, a notable ambiguity: is he driven by fate or driving it? 'Inglorious Arts of Peace' echoes Virgil's 'ignobilis oti' (Georgics 4.564), Virgil's description of his own leisure as a poet while Octavian fought abroad; Marvell reverses the Virgilian contrast, since the poet's leisure is now inglorious. The question of whether Cromwell is the instrument of providence or his own ambition recurs throughout the poem.

title: three-fork'd Lightning
short: Cromwell as a thunderbolt bursting from its cloud, modelled on Lucan's simile for Julius Caesar in the Pharsalia.
body: Lucan, Pharsalia 1.151-57, compares Caesar to lightning forced out by the winds through the clouds, which strikes its own temples and scatters destruction where it falls and returns. Marvell's lightning likewise first breaks through 'his own Side', the cloud that nursed it, then burns through palaces and temples. Jove's three-forked bolt (trisulcum fulmen) is a common classical image. Lucan's poem, a lament for the Roman republic destroyed by Caesar, had been translated by Thomas May (1627), so the source lends the praise an unsettling resonance.

title: through his own Side / The Emulous or Enemy
short: Cromwell overcame rivals within the Parliamentary cause as well as royalist enemies; to hem him in is worse than to oppose him.
body: Cromwell displaced or outmanoeuvred Parliamentarian commanders such as the Earl of Manchester and the Earl of Essex (the Self-Denying Ordinance, 1645), and in 1649 crushed the Leveller mutiny. 'Emulous' means rival, ambitious competitor. For 'Courage high' an emulous ally and an enemy are the same thing, and 'to inclose', to confine such a man within limits, provokes more than outright opposition. The lightning image of the cloud split from within fits this exactly.

title: Caesar's head blasted through his Laurels
short: Lightning struck the King's head through his laurel crown, though laurel was believed to be proof against lightning.
body: 'Caesars head' is Charles I's, the royal 'Caesar'. Ancient lore held that laurel is never struck by lightning; Suetonius reports that Tiberius wore a laurel wreath in thunderstorms for that reason (Tiberius 69), and Pliny records the belief (Natural History 15.134-35). Marvell's lightning penetrates even the protective laurel, the emblem of victory and of royal majesty. The ambiguity is sharp: in Lucan Cromwell's model is Caesar, but here Charles is 'Caesar', so the poem gives the name to both.

title: private Gardens ... the Bergamot
short: Before the wars Cromwell lived retired, as if his highest ambition were to grow a choice pear; the 'bergamot' was the 'pear of kings'.
body: Cromwell was a modest country gentleman in Huntingdon, St Ives and Ely before entering national politics in the 1640s. The bergamot was a fine variety of pear; its name was popularly derived from Turkish beg-armudi, 'the lord's (prince's) pear', which allows a pun: his 'plot' (garden plot and scheme) was to plant a royal pear, that is, perhaps to grow into kingship. Critics differ on whether 'As if' exonerates him or hints at hidden ambition. The retired gardener who saves the state recalls the Roman Cincinnatus.

title: the great Work of Time
short: The ancient monarchy is a structure built by time itself; Cromwell's 'industrious Valour' pulls it down and recasts the kingdom.
body: 'Ruine' is a verb: to destroy. The kingdom is a building (the 'great Work of Time') and then metal recast 'Into another Mold', a metaphor from casting or minting. The admiring and the appalled readings are both available: Brooks heard irony and regret here, while Bush insisted the praise of Cromwell is straightforward. The phrase 'Kingdome old' (l. 35) stresses antiquity: what is destroyed is not only Charles but centuries of constitutional history, which a single man undoes by labour and courage.

title: Justice against Fate; antient Rights
short: Justice may protest, and the King's 'antient Rights' be pleaded, but rights stand or fall according to power.
body: The lines state a de facto view of political authority: rights 'hold or break / As Men are strong or weak'. John Wallace related the poem to the Engagement controversy of 1649-50, in which writers argued that obedience was owed to whatever power actually governed. The stanza can be read as cold realism, as Hobbesian (Leviathan appeared in 1651), or as bitter irony; the legal language ('plead', 'antient Rights') remembers the constitutional case against Cromwell even as it is overruled.

title: Nature hates emptiness, allows less penetration
short: Two principles of natural philosophy: nature abhors a vacuum, and two bodies cannot occupy the same place.
body: The Aristotelian doctrine that there can be no void (horror vacui; Physics 4.6-9) is paired with the impenetrability of bodies: nature 'allows of penetration less', permits two things in one space even less than it tolerates empty space. So when a 'greater Spirit' comes, something must give way. The political vacuum left by the old order will be filled, and Cromwell's spirit physically displaces the King's. The argument dresses political necessity as physical law.

title: Hampton Court and Carisbrooke
short: Charles I escaped from Hampton Court in November 1647 and ended in confinement at Carisbrooke Castle on the Isle of Wight; Marvell suggests Cromwell engineered it.
body: Charles fled Hampton Court on 11 November 1647 and gave himself up on the Isle of Wight, where he was held in Carisbrooke Castle. Royalists and others alleged that Cromwell had frightened him into flight with rumours of assassination so as to get him into a closer prison; Marvell adopts the rumour, praising Cromwell's 'wiser Art' of 'twining subtile fears with hope'. 'Case' means enclosure, cage, with a hunting overtone ('chase'). Historians do not accept that Cromwell planned the flight.

title: The Royal Actor and the Tragick Scaffold
short: The execution of Charles I (30 January 1649) staged as a tragedy, the King as actor and the soldiers as applauding audience.
body: Charles was beheaded on a scaffold built outside the Banqueting House, Whitehall. The theatrical metaphor is double-edged: 'Actor' means both performer and agent; 'adorn' makes the King an ornament to the stage; the soldiers' 'bloody hands' clapping make the audience brutal. The 'Scene' (l. 58) continues the metaphor. Royalist propaganda, especially Eikon Basilike (1649), presented Charles as a martyr, and Milton's Eikonoklastes attacked that theatre of sympathy; Marvell gives the King a dignified exit while keeping the stage frame.

anchor: He nothing common did or mean
title: He nothing common did or mean
short: The famous tribute to Charles's dignity at his execution: he did nothing vulgar, tested the axe's edge with his eye, and bowed his head as onto a bed.
body: Contemporary accounts of the execution record the King's composure and his concern with the block and the axe. 'Keener Eye' makes his glance sharper than the blade. He did not call the gods to 'vindicate' (avenge, defend) his 'helpless Right' with 'vulgar spight', and bowed his 'comely Head' as if to sleep. These eight lines, at the exact centre of the poem, are its emotional climax, and critics are divided over whether they undercut the praise of Cromwell or display Marvell's even-handed Horatian magnanimity toward the vanquished.

anchor: A bleeding Head where they begun
title: The bleeding Head on the Capitol
short: When the foundations of the Capitol were dug, a human head was found, taken as an omen that Rome would be head of the world.
body: Livy (1.55) tells that while Tarquin was clearing the Capitoline hill for the temple of Jupiter, a human head with its face intact was uncovered, which seers read as a sign that the place would be the head (caput) of an empire; Pliny repeats the story. Marvell adds the blood. The King's severed head becomes the founding omen of the new republic, 'the forced Pow'r' assured by that 'memorable Hour'. The pun on caput/Capitol and the blood make the omen grimly ambiguous: the new state is founded on a killing.

anchor: And now the Irish are asham'd
title: The Irish 'tamed'
short: Cromwell's Irish campaign (Aug. 1649-May 1650), including the massacres at Drogheda and Wexford; the conquered are said to praise him.
body: Cromwell landed at Dublin in August 1649, stormed Drogheda (September) and Wexford (October) with the killing of garrisons and many civilians, and returned in May 1650 leaving the conquest to others. The claim that the Irish themselves 'confest / How good he is, how just' has been read as straightforward English Protestant triumphalism, as conventional panegyric, or as savage irony. Critics including Brooks emphasised the irony; historians note that English opinion widely celebrated the campaign.

title: How fit he is to sway / That can so well obey
short: The classical maxim that only one who knows how to obey is fit to rule; Cromwell remains the servant of the Republic.
body: Aristotle's Politics (3.4, 1277b) says that a good citizen must know both how to rule and how to be ruled, and the maxim was a commonplace. In 1650 Cromwell was still a general serving Parliament ('still in the Republick's hand'). 'Sway' means rule. The stanza both praises his obedience and implies his fitness to rule, so that the compliment anticipates the future Protectorate (1653).

anchor: He to the Common Feet presents
title: the Common Feet ... the Publick's skirt
short: Cromwell lays his conquest at the feet of the Commonwealth, like a tenant paying rent, and his sword at the hem of its robe.
body: 'The Common' plays on the Commons and the Commonwealth. Ireland is presented as 'his first years rents', the first year's yield paid by a tenant to the landlord. He 'forbears' (refrains from claiming) his fame, and lays sword and spoils at the 'Publick's skirt', the hem of the personified Republic's garment, a gesture of homage. The feudal language of rents and homage oddly reasserts hierarchy within a republic.

title: the Falcon and the Falconer
short: Cromwell is a trained falcon who, after the kill, perches nearby and returns to the falconer's lure: the Republic still controls him.
body: In falconry the hawk stoops on its prey, kills, and is recalled by the falconer swinging the 'lure', a bunch of feathers on a cord. Marvell's falcon does not 'search' for more prey but perches on the next 'green Bow' (bough), where the falconer 'has her sure'. The simile praises Cromwell's obedience but also implies the danger: a falcon is a predator, controlled only so long as it consents.

title: Caesar, Hannibal, Clymacterick
short: Cromwell will be a Caesar to France and a Hannibal to Italy, a decisive and fatal 'climacteric' to all states not free.
body: Julius Caesar conquered Gaul (58-50 BC), and Hannibal invaded Italy (218 BC); the prophecy imagines Cromwell carrying the Protestant republic's war to Catholic France and Rome. A 'climacteric' was a critical year in a person's life (every seventh or ninth year, the 63rd being the 'grand climacteric'), when great change or death was expected; Cromwell will be such a turning point for monarchies. The name 'Caesar', earlier applied to Charles, is now transferred to Cromwell.

title: The Pict ... party-colour'd Mind ... Plad
short: The Scots, called Picts with a pun on Latin picti (painted), have divided, 'parti-coloured' minds and will hide under their plaid.
body: The Romans named the northern tribes Picti, 'painted men', from their body paint. Marvell puns: the Scots' minds are 'party-colour'd', variegated like tartan and divided by party, since the Covenanters had allied with Charles II while still opposing royalists. They will shrink under the 'Plad' (plaid) and hide in the bracken like deer, hoping the English hunter mistakes them for game. Cromwell's invasion began on 22 July 1650 and he defeated the Scots at Dunbar on 3 September.

title: the Wars and Fortunes Son
short: Cromwell as child of war and fortune; cf. Horace's phrase 'Fortunae filius', a phrase that can flatter or mock.
body: Horace, Satires 2.6.49, describes the envious crowd calling a lucky man 'Fortunae filius', 'Fortune's son'. The phrase stresses luck rather than merit, and fortune is notoriously fickle. 'March indefatigably on' turns the stanza from description to exhortation, almost a soldier's command; the long Latinate adverb fills most of the line and enacts unwearied marching. Critics who read the Ode ironically point to this phrase as a reminder that Cromwell's power rests on chance and war rather than law.

title: Still keep thy Sword erect
short: The upright sword, its hilt making a cross, frightens away the ghosts of the night; it must also be kept ready for use.
body: An upturned sword hilt forms a cross, believed to ward off evil spirits. Classical heroes draw swords against the shades: Odysseus keeps the dead off with his sword (Odyssey 11.48-50), and the Sibyl orders Aeneas to draw his blade on entering the underworld (Aeneid 6.260). The 'Spirits of the shady Night' may be the ghost of the King and the disaffected spirits of royalism. 'For the last effect' means to the final outcome.

anchor: The same Arts that did gain
title: The same Arts that did gain / A Pow'r
short: Power must be kept by the same means that won it, a maxim from Sallust, and a famously ambiguous last word on Cromwell's rule by force.
body: Sallust, Catiline 2.4, says that power is easily kept by the arts by which it was first won ('imperium facile iis artibus retinetur, quibus initio partum est'). The maxim was also associated with Machiavelli's Prince. Applied to Cromwell, whose power was won by the sword, the closing couplet can be read as realistic advice, as approving, or as a warning that a regime founded on force must forever rely on force.

anchor: Much to the Man is due
title: Praise or irony? The critical debate
short: Whether the Ode celebrates Cromwell or quietly criticises him is the central critical question, famously argued by Cleanth Brooks and Douglas Bush.
body: 'And, if we would speak true, / Much to the Man is due' sounds like a concession wrung from a reluctant speaker. Brooks's close reading (1946) found a poised irony, with admiration for Cromwell's force balanced by sympathy for Charles. Bush (1952) replied that such irony is a modern projection and that a 1650 reader would take the praise straight. Later historicist work (Wallace 1968; Worden 1987) set the poem in the debates over allegiance to the new regime. 'Tis Madness to resist or blame' (l. 25) makes resistance to Cromwell resistance to heaven's lightning.
